item.title: Police continue probe into two FICAC officers linked to Charlie Charters case
item.description: POLICE have confirmed that investigations into two former Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption (FICAC) officers linked to the alleged disclosure of confidential internal FICAC information to Charlie Charters are continuing. Assistant Commissioner of Police Crime Loraini Seru told The Fiji Times : “The investigation into the other two continues.”
item.content:encoded:
POLICE have confirmed that investigations into two former Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption (FICAC) officers linked to the alleged disclosure of confidential internal FICAC information to Charlie Charters are continuing.

Assistant Commissioner of Police Crime Loraini Seru told The Fiji Times : “The investigation into the other two continues.”

The matter was referred to Police by FICAC under section 13F of the FICAC Act following allegations concerning the disclosure of official information.

On June 30, FICAC said any decision on whether former FICAC officers would face charges would rest with Police.

The update comes after the High Court permanently stayed the criminal proceedings against citizen journalist Charlie Charters.

In its ruling, the High Court stayed the charges against Mr Charters because of issues relating to the State’s case and FICAC’s conduct in bringing the proceedings.

The two FICAC officers in question were accused of divulging internal information to Mr Charters without written authorisation, violating Section 13G (1) of the FICAC Act.

Police did not provide further details, with no charges announced at this stage.

item.description: THE two sureties for a man accused of attempted murder have been ordered to appear before the High Court after he failed to attend court as required under his bail conditions. item.content:encoded:
THE two sureties for a man accused of attempted murder have been ordered to appear before the High Court after he failed to attend court as required under his bail conditions.

Prosecutor Hezekiah Nofaga informed Justice Dane Tuiqereqere that Saimoni Rokotunidau, who is charged with the attempted murder of Police Constable Senoveva Tikoduadua, remained at large and had also sold the property where he had been residing.

The State applied for the sureties to be summoned to explain Mr Rokotunidau’s non-attendance.

Justice Tuiqereqere granted the application and directed the two sureties to appear on August 25.

Mr Rokotunidau is charged in relation to an incident in April in which Constable Tikoduadua was allegedly struck by a vehicle while manning a police checkpoint in Laqere, Nasinu.

The police officer is the daughter of Defence and Veterans Affairs Minister Pio Tikoduadua.

Mr Rokotunidau also faces a count each of unlawful possession of illicit drugs, going equipped for theft, serious assault, and refusing to have his fingerprints and photographs taken.

item.title: Police arrest four
item.description: FOUR people alleged to have unlawful possession of illicit drugs were arrested in Lautoka on Monday following a drug raid by the joint task force. Assistant Commissioner of Police Operations Kasiano Vusonilawe said the joint task force conducted raids at Tavakubu and on Vio Rd, Lautoka on Monday.
item.content:encoded:
FOUR people alleged to have unlawful possession of illicit drugs were arrested in Lautoka on Monday following a drug raid by the joint task force.

Assistant Commissioner of Police Operations Kasiano Vusonilawe said the joint task force conducted raids at Tavakubu and on Vio Rd, Lautoka on Monday.

During the first raid at Tavakubu, an 18-year-old student and a 24-year-old man were allegedly found in possession of white substances believed to be methamphetamine.

Both were taken into custody and the seized substances were sent for analysis.

In the second raid on Vio Rd, a 38-year-old man and a 37-year-old woman were arrested after several plastics containing white substances believed to be illicit drugs were allegedly discovered.

Cash in local and foreign currencies believed to be the proceeds of crime were also seized.

Mr Vusonilawe said the success of the raids were the result of intelligence sharing and tips received from members of the public who are urged to report suspected drug-related activities through the toll-free number 1681.

item.title: Chamber calls for better security
item.description: MEMBERS of the Sigatoka business community are calling for stronger security for communities in the area following the death of 38-year-old Vimal Nand on Sunday. Nadroga Navosa Chamber of Commerce and Industries president Sailesh Naidu said it was unfortunate that a dispute had escalated to a point where a man’s life was taken away from his family.
item.content:encoded:
MEMBERS of the Sigatoka business community are calling for stronger security for communities in the area following the death of 38-year-old Vimal Nand on Sunday.

Nadroga Navosa Chamber of Commerce and Industries president Sailesh Naidu said it was unfortunate that a dispute had escalated to a point where a man’s life was taken away from his family.

Mr Naidu, who is a close friend of the victim, said he was devastated by Mr Nand’s tragic death.

“We worked together at Warwick Hotels, and I remember him being a very friendly and kind man with a warm heart,” said Mr Naidu.

“He was always smiling and always made an effort to stop and talk to people.

“This is a big loss for his family, his community and for the Sigatoka people.”

Mr Naidu said the suspects must be dealt with the full brunt of the law.

“We demand justice for Vimal’s family and his wife and children.

“This type of outlawed behaviour must not be tolerated at all. We can’t let people with this type of attitude roam our community and attack innocent people without any legitimate and valid reason.

“A life has been taken away. A father and a husband. There should be some kind of justice given to his family and close friends.”

According to police, the suspects confronted the victim, his son and another student while they were out horse riding.

Mr Nand was later found unconscious by his brother with serious head injuries.

He was transferred to the Sigatoka Hospital then to Nadi and later to the Lautoka Hospital where he later died despite attempts to revive him.

item.title: State argues against trio’s bid
item.description: THE State has urged the High Court to reject no-case-to-answer submissions by three former government ministers, arguing evidence from 14 prosecution witnesses is sufficient for the charges to proceed. Assistant Director of Public Prosecutions Laisani Tabuakuro yesterday argued evidence existed that former health minister Dr Neil Sharma allegedly interfered with the medical equipment tender proces
item.content:encoded:
THE State has urged the High Court to reject no-case-to-answer submissions by three former government ministers, arguing evidence from 14 prosecution witnesses is sufficient for the charges to proceed.

Assistant Director of Public Prosecutions Laisani Tabuakuro yesterday argued evidence existed that former health minister Dr Neil Sharma allegedly interfered with the medical equipment tender process by approaching the permanent secretary for Health to write a letter identifying preferred suppliers, disrupting a process already being handled by the relevant committees.

She also disputed the defence claim that the waivers of two tenders granted by former prime minister Voreqe Bainimarama and former attorney-general Aiyaz Sayed-Khaiyum were lawful, arguing the relevant procurement regulations did not permit their use for the equipment involved.

Ms Tabuakuro also argued there was sufficient evidence that Mr Sayed-Khaiyum had intervened in a FICAC investigation, which was subsequently put on hold and not pursued.

Lawyer Devanesh Sharma, representing Mr Bainimarama and Mr Sayed-Khaiyum, argued the waivers were lawfully made under Regulation 48(4) of the Fiji Procurement Regulations 2010, and there was no evidence of prejudice.

On the obstruction charge, he said witnesses had rejected any direction by Mr Sayed-Khaiyum to halt the investigation.

Representing Dr Sharma, Wylie Clarke said the State had failed to prove that his client breached a statutory requirement or possessed the criminal intention required for the charges.

Mr Clarke argued the State’s case largely relied on procurement documents whose contents had not been properly proved, with missing records and faded memories further weakening evidence relating to tenders conducted about 15 years ago.

Justice Usaia Ratuvili will deliver his ruling on October 1.

item.title: Bank to release funds
item.description: THE High Court in Suva has ordered the release of $150,000 from a woman’s frozen bank account after finding that she and her family needed funds to meet their daily needs. Acting Justice Penijamini Lomaloma made the release of funds order on August 6 after considering an application by FICAC to restrain property and funds belonging to Raijieli Naituku Chand, which is allegedly linked to tainted pr
item.content:encoded:
THE High Court in Suva has ordered the release of $150,000 from a woman’s frozen bank account after finding that she and her family needed funds to meet their daily needs.

Acting Justice Penijamini Lomaloma made the release of funds order on August 6 after considering an application by FICAC to restrain property and funds belonging to Raijieli Naituku Chand, which is allegedly linked to tainted property under the Proceeds of Crime Act.

The court had previously ordered the freezing of Mrs Chand’s BRED Bank account after FICAC presented evidence that funds in the account were allegedly tainted property.

The court heard that more than $1.3 million was held in that account, while about $322,468.09 had been received by her husband, Steven Chand.

Justice Lomaloma noted that the couple had several grandchildren, nieces, and nephews to support and no source of income.

The court also heard Mr Chand had a serious medical condition requiring overseas surgery and electronic medical equipment, which was in FICAC’s possession.

Justice Lomaloma said the restraining order had been granted on the lower threshold of reasonable grounds for suspecting that property was tainted, rather than on the balance of probabilities.

He found that justice required some funds to be released to the respondents to meet their needs.

BRED Bank was ordered to immediately release $150,000 to Mrs Chand, with the remaining funds in the account to remain frozen unless further orders are issued by the court.

The court also ordered FICAC to return the medical equipment belonging to Mr Chand immediately.

item.title: Authorities on alert over nitazene drug threat
item.description: AUTHORITIES are stepping up vigilance against nitazenes, a highly potent class of synthetic opioids that Pacific law enforcement agencies fear could make their way into the region. Although Fiji Police have confirmed that nitazenes have not yet entered Fiji, authorities say measures are in place to detect and prevent the potentially deadly substances from crossing the country’s borders.
item.content:encoded:
AUTHORITIES are stepping up vigilance against nitazenes, a highly potent class of synthetic opioids that Pacific law enforcement agencies fear could make their way into the region.

Although Fiji Police have confirmed that nitazenes have not yet entered Fiji, authorities say measures are in place to detect and prevent the potentially deadly substances from crossing the country’s borders.

New Zealand Police senior liaison officer for the Pacific, Superintendent Nicholas Brown said law enforcement agencies across the region, together with immigration and customs authorities, were working to prevent nitazenes and fentanyl from reaching Pacific communities.

“We can’t afford for that to happen,” Superintendent Brown said.

He said New Zealand Police were strengthening their international law enforcement presence, including through senior liaison officers based in Colombia and the United Arab Emirates, while also working with Pacific countries to build resilience against organised crime and illicit drugs.

Superintendent Brown said the police commissioners of New Zealand and Fiji had agreed to trial a localised version of New Zealand’s Resistance to Organised Crime program in Fiji.

The initiative is intended to strengthen community resilience and encourage communities to play a greater role in protecting themselves from organised crime and the harmful effects of illicit drugs.

“It empowers communities to look after and protect themselves, make themselves more resilient and resistant to substances coming in.”

Nitazenes are a group of synthetic opioids that were originally developed decades ago as potential alternatives to morphine. According to information from the University of New South Wales National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, they were never formally introduced for medical use because of their high risk of overdose.

Their emergence in illicit drug markets has raised concern internationally because some nitazenes can be extremely potent and may be present in counterfeit tablets or other illicit substances.

Superintendent Brown said detecting the drugs at borders could be particularly challenging.

“It could be anything, to be honest. It can be powders, it can be pills, it can be liquids,” he said.

Organised criminal groups, he said, continually changed the ways they attempted to move drugs across borders, making cooperation between police, customs and immigration authorities critical.

But he also stressed that law enforcement could not monitor every situation on its own.

“We need the likes of civil society, the churches, we need to work together,” he said.

Fiji Police confirmed that nitazenes have so far not broken through Fiji’s borders.

Police said officers had access to portable detection equipment, including the 1st defender and portable detection kits, which could provide initial indications of the possible presence of a substance.

Any suspected substance is then sent to the forensics laboratory for further testing.

Police said officers working in environments where they may encounter dangerous substances were provided with basic protective equipment, including gloves and masks, while forensic officers were equipped with personal protective equipment suits.

“Awareness is being made on the harmful effects of all drugs, fake or genuine,” police said.

The warning comes as regional authorities remain concerned about the movement of increasingly potent synthetic opioids through international drug-trafficking networks.

No nitazenes on Fiji’s essential medicines list

Fiji Medical Association executive member and FMA representative to the Fiji Medical Council, Dr Alipate Vakamocea said medicines entering Fiji were subject to strict regulation through the relevant government processes and the Fijian Medicinal Products Board.

“From the point of view of Government, that’s not a drug that’s on our essential drug listing,” he said.

The focus on nitazenes comes as Pacific countries seek to strengthen their defences against synthetic opioids, including fentanyl, amid growing international concern about the spread of highly potent illicit substances.

In Fiji, authorities say preventing these substances from entering the country will require more than border controls alone, with police emphasising the importance of cooperation between government agencies, communities, churches and civil society.

Under Fiji law, unauthorised possession, manufacture, supply, import or export of the drug carries a maximum penalty of a $1million fine or life imprisonment.

Authorities are continuing to monitor developments and strengthen their capacity to identify potentially dangerous synthetic opioids before they reach Fiji communities.

item.title: BACK IN HISTORY | Herbal fix for Salote
item.description: A report on how a 52-year-old village woman relied on ‘bush medicine’ to care for her family after the death of her husband was published in The Fiji Times on Saturday, May 1, 1999. It stated that while many people were only beginning to hear about herbal medicines, Salote Koroi was already steadfast in her belief in the land, the environment and its natural resources.
item.content:encoded:
A report on how a 52-year-old village woman relied on ‘bush medicine’ to care for her family after the death of her husband was published in The Fiji Times on Saturday, May 1, 1999.

It stated that while many people were only beginning to hear about herbal medicines, Salote Koroi was already steadfast in her belief in the land, the environment and its natural resources.

Mrs Koroi looked to the environment as a source of life, food, water, shelter, clothing, and life-saving plants and herbs. From an early age, she had lived close to the land.

“It was from the days of my fathers and forefathers that I had love for my land, and the wonderful gifts it has to offer us,” she said.

“It was only a matter of going to the bushes and picking them from here and there, a pound, a squash, a bit of heat, and there you have it — a natural medicine as good, even better than the ones prescribed in the pharmacies.”

Mrs Koroi agreed with the South Pacific Action Committee for Human Ecology and Environment which said that women’s extensive knowledge was often overlooked by Western science.

“People are more concerned about what we do at home; they don’t really come into our homes and see what we are actually doing.”

“They only look at women washing dishes, women looking after children and women cleaning the house.”

She said women were the masters of the home because they carried out most of the work around the house.

“It is easy to get into a pair of jeans and shirt, go out and work in a factory or something.”

Her knowledge of traditional medicine helped her overcome many challenges after her husband died in 1980. Although she initially believed she would not be able to raise her children alone, she succeeded in sending her three sons to school.

“Life is not easy when you live in a village. Travelling to the hospital is rather hard during nights and in times of misfortune.”

“Natural medicines that can be made from guava leaves, wee barks and roots and other herbs are amazing because first they are free and secondly, they work,” Mrs Koroi said.

The article highlighted the use of guava leaves for stomach aches, constipation and bronchial infections, while scraped and pounded wee bark was used to treat flu, fever and chest pains. It concluded that Mrs Koroi’s experience demonstrated that traditional remedies continued to provide effective, free healthcare for village families.
